narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the admission model estimated that you have a 56% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. In other words, based on the factors considered, you were judged slightly more likely to fail than to pass—an unacceptable risk for admission.

The most influential factor was your academic standing in the third year of your undergraduate degree. You ranked in the very bottom group (the first decile), while students who were accepted typically placed around the sixth decile. This ranking pushed strongly toward a prediction of failure. Similarly, your first-year class standing was also in the bottom group, and although this mattered less than your third-year standing, it also pushed toward failure. Together, these two rankings suggest a pattern of academic difficulty that the model weighed heavily.

Your LSAT score, however, worked in the opposite direction. At 40, it was above the average of about 37 among accepted students, and this was the second most important factor overall. It pushed toward passing the exam and helped your case, but it was not enough to overcome the two weak class-rank indicators.

The best next step is to strengthen your academic record before reapplying. Consider completing additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program to earn higher grades, and seek a fresh academic reference. If possible, wait to reapply until you have a sustained record of strong performance, because improving your class standing is the most direct way to change a future decision.
